title: Size Really Matters
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece makes the case for small teams by way of Genghis Khan's decimal military organisation, units of ten, hundred, thousand and ten thousand, each with a leader reporting upward. The historical device is used to argue that the building-block of ten produced cohesion, skill and battlefield flexibility, and that the same logic survives a thousand years later. The mechanisms it names are specific rather than atmospheric: smaller teams improve speed of communication, clarity of expectations and the in-time feedback that improvement depends on. Two further effects are attributed to size directly, that individual accountability falls as group size rises, and that larger groups encourage social loafing. Contemporary benchmarks are supplied, an effective range of four to ten, Google's preference for four to seven, and Amazon's two-pizza rule at around ten. The closing construction is the memorable one, an organisation built as a team of teams so that it looks big from outside and feels small from inside, with coordination and trust following from the felt smallness.
points: The operating recommendation is concrete: default to four to ten people, with Google at four to seven and Amazon's two-pizza rule as convergent evidence from very different organisations.
The mechanisms are named rather than assumed, smaller teams improving speed of communication, clarity of expectations and the timeliness of feedback.
Two effects are attributed to size itself: individual accountability falls as the group grows, and larger groups make social loafing easier to hide inside.
The team-of-teams construction is the piece's practical answer to scale, letting an enterprise look big on the outside while feeling small on the inside.
The Khan example does real work rather than decorating the argument, showing a decimal building-block producing cohesion and battlefield flexibility under the hardest possible test.
quotes: Good leaders intuitively know that big teams are rarely close-knit, nor do they possess the flexibility necessary to adapt to changing conditions.

By breaking down larger collections of people into smaller and more manageable teams, leaders can improve just about every aspect necessary for high performance, including speed of communication, clarity of expectations, and the in-time feedback critical for improvement.
Experienced leaders also know that the larger the group, the lower the individual accountability.
It is not surprising, then, to learn that the average team size in the most effective organizations is between 4-10 team members.
The leaders at Amazon believe a team should never be larger than what two pizzas can feed, or about 10 people.
Organizations and teams that feel and act small promote higher coordination and trust.
